title: Voices from the frontier
description: Eight 90-second opening excerpts. One useful next step.

reels.speaker: Chris Hadfield
reels.headline: Confidence has a practice session.
reels.title: What I learned from going blind in space | Chris Hadfield | TED
reels.takeaway: Preparation can make an intimidating situation more manageable. Rehearsing what might go wrong is part of learning to do something difficult.
reels.prompt: Choose one failure. Trace what you would notice and what you would do next.

excerpt.label: Opening 90 seconds
excerpt.selection: Opening excerpt, not a selected highlight.

reels.speaker: Mae Jemison
reels.headline: Bring your whole imagination.
reels.title: Mae Jemison on teaching arts and sciences together
reels.takeaway: Your writing, art and science classes can develop different parts of the same imagination. A technical idea becomes more useful when you can explain why it matters.
reels.prompt: Give one engineering choice a clear explanation that someone outside the field can understand.

lesson.title: Write the paragraph that changes the drawing

excerpt.label: Opening 90 seconds
excerpt.selection: Opening excerpt, not a selected highlight.

reels.speaker: Adam Steltzner & the JPL team
reels.headline: Big leaps are made of small decisions.
reels.title: 7 Minutes of Terror: The Challenges of Getting to Mars
reels.takeaway: An audacious landing becomes a sequence of jobs, measurements and handoffs. Every part has to work with the parts around it.
reels.prompt: Draw the handoff between two subsystems. Name what each one needs from the other.

lesson.title: Find the gap between two finished parts

excerpt.label: Opening 90 seconds

reels.speaker: Gwynne Shotwell
reels.headline: The mission needs your skills.
reels.title: Engineering America: Gwynne Shotwell at TEDxChapmanU
reels.takeaway: A big mission needs people who can calculate, build, communicate and solve the next concrete problem. Coursework can be a place to begin developing those abilities.
reels.prompt: Pick one skill from this semester and give it a small, physical job.

project.title: Build a service bay from cardboard

reels.speaker: Peter Beck
reels.headline: Small can open a very large door.
reels.title: Small rockets are the next space revolution | Peter Beck
reels.takeaway: A smaller machine can serve a different need. Start by identifying the job, then choose a scale you can build, measure and improve.
reels.prompt: Ask which modest test would remove the most uncertainty from your next design.

lesson.title: Spend the next hour where it teaches most

reels.speaker: Vijay Kumar
reels.headline: The movement starts with an idea.
reels.title: Robots that fly ... and cooperate | Vijay Kumar
reels.takeaway: Spectacular motion has quiet foundations: geometry, sensing and feedback. You can start investigating those ideas with two links on a sheet of paper.
reels.prompt: Predict an arm's endpoint, build its pose and compare the measurement with the prediction.

lesson.title: Place the fingertip with two joints

reels.speaker: Sylvia Earle
reels.headline: Exploration comes with responsibility.
reels.title: TED Prize wish: Protect our oceans - Sylvia Earle
reels.takeaway: Exploration and care belong together. Understanding an environment can change what you choose to build there, and how you decide whether it should be built.
reels.prompt: Name one consequence your design could have beyond its immediate technical job.

lesson.title: Understand the pressure of the deep

project.title: Explain a design decision and its consequences

reels.speaker: Demis Hassabis
reels.headline: A model can become a way to discover.
reels.title: How AI Is Unlocking the Secrets of Nature and the Universe | Demis Hassabis | TED
reels.takeaway: A model can help people ask new scientific questions. Build the habit of testing predictions and noticing what the available evidence does not establish.
reels.prompt: Write down a prediction before measuring, then keep the result even if it surprises you.

lesson.title: Change one thing you can explain
